title: Subject pronouns, tu vs vous
goal: By the end of this lesson you can use all the French subject pronouns, choose between tu and vous in real Quebec situations, and use on the way people actually speak.

body: Subject pronouns tell you who does the action. French has nine of them. *je* becomes *j'* before a vowel or silent h: *j'aime*, *j'habite*.
*il* and *elle* replace any masculine or feminine noun, including things: *Le café? Il est chaud.* (The coffee? It's hot.) There is no separate word for 'it'.
learn.tip: One man in a group of 100 women: ils.

body: *tu* is for one person you know well: friends, family, children, classmates, people your age in casual settings. *vous* is for one person you want to be polite with, and for any group of two or more people.

Quebec uses *tu* much more than France does: with coworkers, often with your boss, with younger shop staff, and between strangers of the same age. But *vous* is still expected with older people, in formal service (bank, doctor, government offices) and with anyone you don't know in a formal setting.

head: Situation (Quebec)
Usual choice
rows: often tu, vous is always safe

learn.tip: When unsure, start with vous. If they answer with tu, follow them.

body: In spoken French, *on* almost always replaces *nous* for 'we': *On est à Montréal* = We're in Montreal. *Nous* is used in writing and formal speech.
*On* takes the same verb form as *il* / *elle*: *on est*, *on a*, *on aime*. It can also mean 'people / you in general': *Au Québec, on parle français.*

learn.h: Quebec: nous autres, vous autres, eux autres
body: In Quebec speech, plural pronouns are often reinforced with *autres* to stress the group: *nous autres* (us), *vous autres* (you guys), *eux autres* (them). Typical sentence: *Nous autres, on est de Québec.*
You will also hear *vous autres* as a casual 'you all' in questions: *Vous autres, ça va?* These forms are informal but used by everyone in conversation.
Casual pronunciation also shortens pronouns: *tu es* → *t'es*, *il* → *y*, *elle* → *a* or *è*. You will study these with être next weeks.

examples.note: je → j' before a vowel or silent h
tu: to a friend or someone your age
elle = it, for a feminine noun
il = it, for a masculine noun
nous = we in writing or formal speech

examples.note: Quebec casual: nous autres for emphasis

quebec.intro: Quebecers use on for 'we' and tu with far more people than in France. But vous is still expected with older people and in formal service, so the roadmap's 'tu is the default' needs nuance: tu is very common, vous is always safe.

items.note: on for nous is normal spoken French everywhere

items.qc: Nous autres, on est de Montréal.

items.note: tu es → t'es in casual speech
no change: vous stays with an older stranger in Quebec too

drills.q: Which pronoun do you use with your best friend?
drills.why: tu is for people you know well.

drills.q: Which pronoun do you use to speak to three friends?
drills.why: vous is always used for two or more people.
livre is masculine, so it = il.

drills.q: What does 'on' most often mean in spoken French?
drills.why: On replaces nous in everyday speech.

drills.q: You meet your elderly neighbour for the first time in Quebec. You say…
drills.why: With an older stranger, use vous until invited to say tu.
je → j' before a vowel or silent h.

drills.q: Marie et Julie? ___ sont à l'école. (they)
drills.en: Marie and Julie? They're at school.

drills.q: Paul et Julie? ___ sont à Québec. (they)
drills.en: Paul and Julie? They're in Quebec City.

drills.why: maison is feminine, so it = elle.
tu or vous, masculine or feminine.
On est in speech, nous sommes in writing.
fin is the everyday Quebec word for nice.

Eux autres, y sont en retard.

pron.tip: zhuh; before a vowel just zh: zha-BEET.
Same sound [eel]: listen to the verb to tell them apart.
eel SÕ (are) vs eel ZÕ (have): the liaison changes the meaning.

dialogue.fr: Bonjour, madame. Vous êtes la nouvelle voisine?
dialogue.en: Hello, ma'am. Are you the new neighbour?

dialogue.fr: Oui! Mais on peut se tutoyer. Je m'appelle Sophie.
dialogue.en: Yes! But we can say tu. My name is Sophie.

dialogue.fr: D'accord! Moi, c'est Daniel. Tu es de Montréal?
dialogue.en: OK! I'm Daniel. Are you from Montreal?

dialogue.fr: Non, nous autres, on est de Québec.

dialogue.en: How many of you are there?

dialogue.fr: On est trois: mon mari, ma fille et moi.
dialogue.en: There are three of us: my husband, my daughter and me.

questions.q: Why does Daniel switch from vous to tu?
options: Sophie invites him to say tu

speak.prompt: Say 'Are you ready?' to a friend, to your boss (formal), and to a group.
speak.model: Tu es prêt? / Vous êtes prêt? / Vous êtes prêts?

speak.prompt: Say where you and your family or friends are, using on.
speak.model: On est à Montréal. On est à la maison.

speak.prompt: Ask someone politely if you can say tu.

write.prompt: Write 5 short sentences, each with a different subject pronoun (je, tu, il/elle, on, vous, ils/elles), about people you know.
write.model: Je suis à Laval. Tu es à Montréal. Ma sœur est gentille: elle est professeure. On est à la maison. Mes amis? Ils sont à l'école.

quiz.q: What is 'it' for a feminine noun?
quiz.why: Pronouns follow grammatical gender: la table → elle.
on est, on a: like il / elle.

quiz.q: A group of four women and one man is…
quiz.why: Any masculine member makes the group ils.
Nous autres, on… is common in conversation.
tutoyer = use tu; vouvoyer = use vous.

quiz.q: With a doctor or a government agent in Quebec, use…
'T'es prête?' is a casual form of…

quiz.why: Writing and formal speech use nous.
